title: Two monks and a river
hook: Tanzan carries a woman across a stream, and hours later Ekido is still carrying her in his head (Zen story, Japan)
carry: I set her down at the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nan-in poured tea until it spilled. Your line was empty the cup. Did you listen once today as if you knew nothing yet? Day forty-four.

It's two in the morning, and you're replaying something someone said to you at lunch. Or last week. Or in 2019. They've long forgotten it. They're asleep. And you're still turning it over, holding it, carrying it around the dark room. Everybody knows that feeling. Today's story is about two monks walking home in the rain. Their names were Tanzan and Ekido. The water is high and the road is a mess, and at the crossing stands a young woman in a silk kimono who can't get across. Tanzan does something that his companion will not stop thinking about for hours. Today's story is two monks and a river.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, REPLAYING.` → `TANZAN AND EKIDO.` → `A WOMAN WHO CAN'T CROSS.`

segments.voice: Tanzan doesn't hesitate. Come on, he says. He picks her up in his arms, carries her across the water, sets her down on the other side, and walks on. Ekido says nothing. Not a word, all afternoon, all the way to the temple. But he's boiling. These monks had vowed to keep their distance from women, and his companion just picked one up in the road. Finally, that night, he can't hold it in. We monks aren't supposed to go near women, he says. Especially not young and lovely ones. Why did you do that? And Tanzan answers: I set her down at the river. Are you still carrying her? That's the story. A word on the details: in the oldest English telling, the crossing is a flooded, muddy road; most retellings made it a river, and the river stuck. Tanzan was a real Zen teacher of nineteenth-century Japan, known for being unconventional. Now look who's really carrying the woman. Tanzan held her for a minute, to help, and let her go. Ekido never touched her, and he carried her for hours, in his head, heavier with every step. The weight wasn't in the act. It was in the holding on. That's why this story gets told at kitchen tables and in therapists' offices. The old insult. The awkward moment. The thing you should have said. The thing that was done, and finished, long ago. Zen teachers have a word for letting go, hōge, casting down. The question is Tanzan's: are you still carrying her?
screen: `HE CARRIES HER ACROSS.` · `EKIDO BOILS ALL AFTERNOON.` · `ARE YOU STILL CARRYING HER?` · `THE WEIGHT IS IN THE HOLDING ON.` · then, large: `I SET HER DOWN AT THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one thing you're still carrying. Settle, and breathe. Find something that happened, and is over, but that you're still holding. A remark. A mistake. An argument that ended days ago. Feel where you carry it: shoulders, jaw, stomach. Now picture a river. Picture yourself walking to the far bank, and setting it down on the ground there. You don't have to forget it. Just stop carrying it for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Two monks and a river. One monk carries a woman across and sets her down; the other carries her in his head all day. Today's word.
screen: `TWO MONKS AND A RIVER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I set her down at the river. Today, when an old moment comes back for another round, say it inside, and put it down again. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Zen teachers often tell the story of Tanzan and Ekido when talking about letting go, and in meditation practice people notice a thought they keep returning to and set it down, again and again.

original.note: Japanese, hōge: letting go, casting down, a Zen word for dropping what you're holding.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about monks and rules.
what it means: the weight isn't in the act; it's in the holding on long after it's over.
what a scholar hears: Tanzan was a real nineteenth-century teacher; the oldest English telling has a muddy road, and retellings turned it into a river.

notes: The best-known English version (Zen Flesh, Zen Bones, 'Muddy Road') is not public domain and has a muddy road, not a river; the script says so and paraphrases.
Tanzan (Hara Tanzan, 1819–1892) described as a real, unconventional teacher of 19th-century Japan; confirm. Ekido's historicity not claimed.
Japanese 放下 (hōge; also 放下著 hōgejaku) as the Zen word for letting go: confirm spelling and reading.
Carry has capital I, allowed by the guide ('I').
